subtype: Approach: adjust routines to reduce stress while waiting [Revision]
passage:
The scan results were due on Friday, and Aadhya's internal exams started on Wednesday. Every night around midnight she scrolled through health pages, and every night her chest tightened a little more. On Sunday she saw the pattern: the more she read, the worse she felt, and the less she studied.

So she made new rules. Lights out by eleven. A brisk walk round the hostel lawn each evening. One fifteen-minute search at five o'clock, phone left on the desk afterwards. Her brother Pradeep called at nine to check she had eaten. By Tuesday she was sleeping better and revising in short, steady blocks, still nervous about Friday but no longer spinning.

qa.q: What time was Aadhya's daily search allowed to happen?
qa.a: Once a day, for fifteen minutes at five o'clock.

qa.q: What was Aadhya afraid of on those midnight scrolling nights, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Aadhya feared bad news from the scan, and her chest tightening a little more each night shows how fear grew.

qa.q: If a night-time urge to search came back anyway, what could Aadhya try, and why?
qa.a: She could jot the worry in a notebook to raise with the doctor on Friday, because it sets the thought aside without feeding it. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Aadhya's new routine?
qa.a: Pradeep, calling each evening, might see a sister who is steadier and eating properly, and feel relieved that his check-in fits into her plan.

grounding: A person sees that night-time scrolling raises fear, then fixes bedtime, walks, and limits searching while waiting for results.

subtype: Approach: follow the treatment plan with a reminder routine [Action]
passage:
Note for the staff file, written by Gurpreet, print-shop floor supervisor.

Maria came back on Monday after her diagnosis and told me, without fuss, what the doctor had asked her to do. She wrote it in a small notebook while we talked. Over the next few days I saw her set phone alarms for her next visit and the tests, and she keeps a blue folder of reports in her locker. When an alarm rings during a job, she steps aside for a minute, then returns.

I adjusted her Thursday shift so she can reach the clinic. I have not asked her about details and will not unless she brings them up. She looks tired some days but organised.

qa.q: Where does Maria keep her folder of reports?
qa.a: In her locker, and it is a blue folder.

qa.q: What might Maria be feeling when she steps aside for a minute as an alarm rings?
qa.a: She likely feels responsible and determined, taking her instructions seriously even if tired, and wanting to stay on top of care.

qa.q: What could Maria do if she missed an alarm one day, and why?
qa.a: She could check her notebook and folder and phone the clinic to rebook, because a routine has backups and a missed reminder is not the end of it.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet's Thursday change affect Maria?
qa.a: It gives Maria a way to keep her appointments without choosing between work and care, and not being questioned about details respects her privacy. 🙂

grounding: After a diagnosis, a person writes down the doctor's instructions, sets phone reminders and keeps reports in a folder.

subtype: Approach: rely on a home remedy from a relative instead of a check-up [Pitfall]
passage:
Anand's cough had hung on since the monsoon, and exams were three weeks away. His uncle Tarun, who ran the hardware shop, looked up from the counter and said, "Take this herbal powder in warm water, it's nothing, we all get this." Anand's mother was away at his aunt's for a wedding, and the clinic in the next town was an hour by bus. Relief flooded in, since he had no time for trouble now.

He drank the powder morning and night. The cough stayed. Two months later he was breathless on the stairs, and he missed the internal test while sitting at the clinic waiting for his turn. The doctor asked why he had not come sooner, and Anand could only say the advice had sounded so calm.

qa.q: What did Tarun tell Anand to take?
qa.a: Tarun said to take herbal powder in warm water.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel relief when his uncle called the cough nothing?
qa.a: Anand was busy and anxious about exams and the long bus ride, so a comforting answer meant he could avoid the trouble of a clinic visit.

qa.q: What else could Anand have done when the cough continued, and why?
qa.a: He could have gone to the doctor, perhaps with a friend or his mother by phone, because the cough was not going away and a check-up would give real facts instead of comfort.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when he learns Anand missed the test?
qa.a: Tarun probably feels guilty or worried, since he meant to reassure and never expected his easy words to delay care.

grounding: A relative's soothing herbal advice replaces a check-up, delaying medical care with a cost to the person.

subtype: Approach: notice the pattern through a mood diary [Thinking]
passage:
For three weeks I felt like a phone on low battery, and I couldn't say why. In my final year, everyone else seemed busy, so I just kept going. Then I started writing three lines each night in the back of my planner: hours slept, what I ate, and a mood out of five.

After fourteen days I looked at the page and thought, wait. The ones and twos all come after nights I slept past three. They also come on days when I spoke to nobody at all. It wasn't random. It wasn't only my thesis either.

I still didn't have an answer, but I had something I could show. I took the planner to Alka, the counsellor, and said, look at this. Tanvir

qa.q: Where did Tanvir write the nightly notes?
qa.a: In the back of a planner.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling before the diary began?
qa.a: Tanvir felt drained and flat, like a phone on low battery, without knowing why, and did not want to bother anyone busy.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do next with the diary pattern, and why?
qa.a: Tanvir could try one change, such as earlier nights, while continuing to write and sharing the page with Alka, because the record shows whether anything shifts.

qa.q: How might Alka, the counsellor, see the planner pages?
qa.a: Alka may find the pages useful because they give concrete detail and a starting point, rather than a vague sense that something is wrong.

grounding: A final-year student records sleep, food and mood daily, sees a link with late nights and isolation, and brings it to a professional.

subtype: Approach: tell a trusted friend or family member [Action]
passage:
Honestly, the first person I told was Joseph. It was a Tuesday after class, and we were on the canteen steps. I said, "Everything has weighed on me for a month now," and my voice came out smaller than I expected. He didn't try to fix anything, he just moved his bag so I could sit. That was it, but my shoulders dropped.

A week later I told my sister on a video call, and she went quiet, then asked what I needed. I said I didn't know yet. She offered to sit with me while I looked for a counsellor at my college. I'm Hansa, and I used to think saying it out loud would make it bigger. It made it smaller.

qa.q: Where were Hansa and Joseph when Hansa first said things felt heavy?
qa.a: On the canteen steps after class on a Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel after telling Joseph, and what shows it?
qa.a: Hansa felt some relief, shown by the shoulders dropping once Joseph made room to sit without trying to fix anything.

qa.q: What could Hansa do with the offer to sit together while looking for a college counsellor, and why would it help?
qa.a: Hansa could accept it, because a step feels easier when someone is beside you.

qa.q: What is it like for Hansa's sister to hear this on a video call?
qa.a: Hansa's sister may feel worried and helpless at a distance, so asking what Hansa needs gives the sister something useful to do.

grounding: A student tells Joseph and later a sister about a heavy month, and saying it aloud reduces isolation.

subtype: Approach: book an appointment with a counsellor or psychiatrist [Action]
passage:
"Did you call?" Afreen asked, closing the hostel door.

"Yes. The college counselling centre. Thursday at four," Tanuja said.

"Proud of you. What will you say?"

"That's the thing. I'll forget it all when I sit down."

"Then write it. Give me your pen."

"Okay. For about a month I've been waking at five and can't get back to sleep. I don't want to eat. Nothing feels fun, even my favourite show."

"Add that you've been skipping the group project calls."

"Right. Should I say it's silly?"

"No. You wouldn't call a broken wrist silly. Just hand them the page."

Tanuja folded the paper into her diary and, for the first time in weeks, let out a long breath.

qa.q: When is Tanuja's session at the counselling centre?
qa.a: On Thursday at four.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja ask whether she should say it was silly?
qa.a: Tanuja feared her problems might seem small or a sign of weakness, so she wanted to be reassured about asking.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja bring to the session, and why?
qa.a: Tanuja could bring a list of questions along with the summary, because it helps her use the time well when nerves make her forget.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel about helping Tanuja write the page?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels glad to help and hopeful, having pushed gently by comparing it to a broken wrist so Tanuja would treat it as normal care.

grounding: A student books a counselling session and writes a short symptom summary, treating professional help as a normal step.

subtype: Approach: push through and hide it [Pitfall]
passage:
Come, sit. I'll tell you about my second year, Ganga. I'm Chaitanya, and back then I thought that if I admitted I was struggling, everyone would look at me differently. So I smiled at breakfast, cracked jokes in the lab, and said 'all fine!' to every message. Then I stopped replying to messages at all.

I skipped lunch most days and told the mess cook I'd eaten. By the fourth week my hands shook in practicals and I couldn't follow a single lecture. Rekha, who shared my bench, knocked on my door one evening and said, 'You're not okay, are you?' I nearly said 'I'm fine' again. It took me another two weeks after that to ask for help, and I lost a whole semester's momentum.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya tell the mess cook?
qa.a: That Chaitanya had eaten, even though lunch was skipped most days.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya afraid of when hiding the struggle?
qa.a: Chaitanya feared that admitting difficulty would make people look at Chaitanya differently, as weak.

qa.q: When Rekha knocked, what different choice could Chaitanya have made, and why?
qa.a: Chaitanya could have let Rekha in and said things were hard, because the knock was an opening, and every week of delay cost more energy.

qa.q: How did Rekha see Chaitanya's cheerful face before that evening?
qa.a: Rekha noticed something was wrong beneath the jokes, as the missed lunches and silence did not fit the smile.

grounding: An elder recalls hiding a struggle behind cheer, skipping meals and ignoring friends, which drained energy and delayed help.

subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]
passage:
Day 4. Tejas woke at noon, the whole to-do list staring at him like a wall. That evening he told himself: if I can't do everything, I shouldn't try to do anything. Then he changed the thought. Just three things tomorrow. Up by eight. A real meal. Ten minutes outside.

Day 9. His roommate Tanuja saw him drinking tea on the balcony at eight-thirty and said nothing, only slid a plate of poha toward him. He whispered to himself, that's two.

Day 16. The list still had only three lines. But he also added a call with his mother, then a short walk to the tea stall. He noted that the small list didn't feel like giving up. It felt like holding on until his energy returned.

qa.q: What three tasks did Tejas set for himself?
qa.a: Up by eight, a real meal and ten minutes outside.

qa.q: What does Tejas's thought on Day 16 about the small list suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: Tejas feels a quiet steadiness and self-acceptance, seeing the short list as holding on rather than failing.

qa.q: What could Tejas do on a day when even three tasks feel too much, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could keep just one, such as a drink of water on the balcony, because a smaller step still keeps the habit and avoids the all-or-nothing trap.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Tejas's change over those days?
qa.a: Tanuja may notice him surfacing slowly, with the plate of poha and the silence being a low-pressure way to show support.

grounding: On low days a person cuts demands to three basic tasks to save energy and gradually rebuilds from there.

subtype: Approach: rely on one person as the only support [Pitfall]
passage:
Vasudha, my roommate, was the only person I told. At first it felt like a relief, and I began to text her every time the low feeling came, then to talk at midnight, and by the second month at all hours. She listened, always, and I never asked her how she was.

Then she began wearing headphones in the room. She stayed late in the library. One evening she said quietly, "I care about you, but I can't be the only one you lean on. I'm running out." I felt as though a door had shut. Later I saw that I had put every low moment on one person, and that made us both feel worse. Ankita

qa.q: What did Vasudha begin wearing in the room?
qa.a: She began wearing headphones in the room.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when Vasudha said she was running out?
qa.a: Ankita felt hurt and rejected, as though a door had shut, before realising later how much had been placed on Vasudha.

qa.q: What could Ankita have done earlier so support was not all on one person, and why?
qa.a: Ankita could have also talked to a counsellor or family, since one person alone cannot hold every difficult moment and may need rest.

qa.q: How does Vasudha experience Ankita's constant reaching out?
qa.a: Vasudha becomes tired and overwhelmed, hiding in headphones and the library, even though she cares.

grounding: A student relies on one roommate for every low moment, and the roommate becomes overwhelmed and withdraws.

subtype: Approach: build a wider support net with roles [Revision]
passage:
Sunday night. Told Ira, my roommate, I was sorry for the past two months, and she said, "Don't apologise, just let's fix it." We talked till ten. It turns out she has been holding this for too long, and I saw it on her face.

So here is the new plan, written down so I stop wriggling out of it. One: book a weekly slot with the college counsellor. Two: a call with Mum and Papa every Sunday, where I say how the week really was. Three: the Saturday walking group by the lake, which Ira said she'd join twice a month. Ira's part is now small and clear: a short check-in text, not a rescue at midnight. I feel lighter already. Yamini

qa.q: On which day is Yamini's weekly call with Mum and Papa?
qa.a: Every Sunday, with Mum and Papa.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel after agreeing the new plan with Ira?
qa.a: Yamini feels lighter and a little guilty, having seen Ira's tiredness and being relieved to share the load more fairly.

qa.q: What could Yamini do if the walking group turned out not to suit Yamini, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could look for another regular activity with people, because the aim is a wider net, and one part can be swapped without losing the rest.

qa.q: How does the new plan change things for Ira?
qa.a: Ira gets a small, clear role of a check-in text rather than midnight rescues, so Ira can stay a friend without burning out.

grounding: After a roommate's fatigue, a student adds a counsellor, a family call and a walking group, each with an agreed role.
